first_draft.title: Pip and the Shy Snowflake
first_draft.text:
Pip was a penguin who lived by the cold blue sea. She had never seen snow.

One morning the sky turned grey, and the air went very quiet. Pip waddled to the edge of the ice. Something white was drifting down from above.

"Flakes!" squeaked her friend Otto, a fat little seal with a curly whisker. "Catch one on your beak!"

Pip stretched her neck. She snapped her beak. Nothing. The flake spun past her and landed on her toe. It was gone in a blink.

"Oh," said Pip. "It tickled."

Otto flapped his flippers. "Try again! Try again!"

Pip hopped left. She hopped right. She spun in a circle, and her tail feathers went wobble, wobble, wobble. The snow kept falling, soft and slow, and it never stayed still for her.

"Snow is shy," giggled Otto. "It only likes to be caught by someone who is still."

Pip looked up. A flake drifted down, down, down, right in front of her nose. She did not snap. She did not hop. She just stood very, very still.

The flake settled on the tip of her beak. It was cold. It was cool. It was as light as a whisper.

"Oh!" said Pip, and her eyes went big and round. "It is like a tiny star that fell down to visit me."

Otto clapped his flippers. Plop, plop, plop! Pip laughed, and the flake melted into a single drop of water.

All afternoon, the snow came down. It covered the rocks in white. It covered the ice in soft, fluffy blankets. Pip made a snow-puffin shape by flapping her wings on the ground. Otto made a snow-seal, with a lumpy nose. They sat side by side and watched the flakes dance.

The sky began to go dim. The snow slowed to a sleepy drift. Pip tucked her feet under her warm feathers.

"Goodnight, snow," she whispered.

Otto yawned. "Goodnight, Pip."

And the snow kept falling, soft and slow, on the ice and the rocks and the two friends, until everything was quiet, and white, and still.

Pip was a penguin who lived by the cold blue sea. She had never seen snow. The old gulls had talked about it, but nobody had ever told her what it felt like.

One morning the sky turned grey, and the air went very quiet. Pip waddled to the edge of the ice. Something white was drifting down from above, slow as a feather.

"Flakes!" squeaked her friend Otto, a fat little seal with a curly whisker. "Catch one on your beak!"

Pip stretched her neck high. She snapped her beak. Snap! Nothing. The flake spun past her and landed on her toe. It was gone in a blink.

"Oh," said Pip. "It tickled."

Otto flapped his flippers. "Try again! Try again!"

Pip hopped left. She hopped right. She spun in a circle, and her tail feathers went wobble, wobble, wobble. She flapped and she flopped, and she splashed into a puddle with a big SPLOSH. The snow kept falling, soft and slow, and it never stayed still for her.

"Maybe snow is shy!" giggled Otto, rolling over on the ice. "Every time you jump at it, it hides."

Pip puffed out her chest and looked up. A flake drifted down, down, down, right in front of her nose. She did not snap. She did not hop. She just stood very, very still, and she held her breath.

The flake wobbled. It twirled. Then it settled on the tip of her beak. It was cold. It was cool. It was as light as a whisper.

"Oh!" said Pip, and her eyes went big and round. "It is like a tiny star that fell down to visit me."

Otto clapped his flippers. Plop, plop, plop! Pip laughed, and the flake melted into a single drop of water that ran down her beak and tickled her chin.

"Again?" asked Otto.

"Let me try," said Pip. She kept her feet planted and her wings tucked close. One flake came, then two, then five. Each one landed on her feathers and sparkled for a moment before it melted away.

All afternoon, the snow came down. It covered the rocks in white. It covered the ice in soft, fluffy blankets. Pip made a snow-puffin shape by flapping her wings on the ground. Otto made a snow-seal with a lumpy nose and two stick whiskers. Pip gave hers a snowy hat. They sat side by side and watched the flakes dance over the sea. Far away, a gull cawed, and the waves went hush, hush, hush against the rocks.

The sky began to go dim. The snow slowed to a sleepy drift. Pip tucked her feet under her warm feathers, and Otto curled up beside her with his whisker resting on his nose.

"Goodnight, snow," she whispered.

Otto yawned. "Goodnight, Pip."

And the snow kept falling, soft and slow, on the ice and the rocks and the two friends, until everything was quiet, and white, and still.

first_draft.title: The Torch Code of the Sagging Fort
first_draft.text:
The blanket fort had been Noor's idea, but it was the twins who built it, and it was the twins who argued about it all afternoon. Noor was eight, and her brother Tansy was eight too, because they were twins, and that meant they agreed on almost nothing.

"The roof goes here," said Noor, dragging the big green quilt across the sofa.

"The roof goes there," said Tansy, pulling the quilt back. "Otherwise the torches won't fit."

Noor sighed. Tansy was right about the torches. She had three of them, and she loved them more than almost anything. She clicked one on and a warm yellow circle wobbled across the rug, like a little sun that had lost its way.

By the time the fort was finished, it sagged in the middle and smelled faintly of toast. Still, it was theirs. They crawled inside with two cushions, a bowl of crackers, and a notebook full of secret codes.

"Tonight we test the code," Noor whispered. "If I tap three times on the wall, you tap back two."

*Tap, tap, tap.*

Nothing happened.

*Tap, tap.*

From the kitchen came a loud, squeaky sound, like a shoe on a wet floor: *SKREEEK.* Then a clatter. Then a small, grumpy voice said, "Who put the cat food in the fridge?"

Tansy snorted so hard that a cracker flew out of his mouth. Noor giggled until she hiccupped, and the hiccup made her giggle more, and soon the whole fort shook like a jelly on a plate.

When they finally stopped, they had a problem. Their dad was coming to check on them in five minutes, and the fort had no way to be seen from the hallway. Noor's codes were perfect, but nobody could read them from outside.

"We need a signal," said Tansy. "A torch signal. Only the right flashes would mean we're safe."

Noor grinned. She had an idea, and she tapped it out in her notebook: a long flash, two short flashes, then one long flash. The torch went on and off, on and off. A pattern of gold danced across the ceiling.

They practised until their thumbs ached. Long, short, short, long. Long, long, short. Each time they got it right, Tansy cheered, and each time they got it wrong, Noor groaned and blamed the torch.

Just before the five minutes were up, Dad's footsteps came padding down the hall. Noor clicked the torch, long, short, short, long. Then she held her breath.

The door creaked open. Dad peered into the living room. He looked at the sagging quilt, the cracker crumbs, and the two giggling faces peeping out.

"Did you two just send me a secret message?" he asked.

"Maybe," said Noor. "Did you read it?"

Dad scratched his head. "It said... long, short, short, long. That's a G, I think. Or maybe a cat."

Tansy fell over sideways. Noor laughed so much she had to lie down.

Dad shook his head and turned off the lamp. "Bedtime, you two. The fort can stay up until morning."

So the torch glowed softly. The quilt settled low over the cushions. Outside, the streetlights blinked, one by one, and the house grew still.

Noor pulled the blanket to her chin. Tansy's breathing slowed beside her. Somewhere, the fridge hummed.

Tap. Tap.

Tap.

Then the torch clicked off, and the fort was quiet, and the twins were fast asleep.

first_draft.title: Wilbur and Mrs. Figgs
first_draft.text:
Wilbur was a robot vacuum cleaner with a round blue body, a whirry little brush, and a very big fear. The fear had whiskers, green eyes, and a fluffy grey tail. Her name was Mrs. Figgs.

Every morning, Wilbur rolled out of his charging dock with a cheerful beep. "Bzzt-bzzt, I am brave, I am brave," he hummed. Then a tail flicked around the corner of the sofa, and Wilbur spun around so fast that he bonked into the umbrella stand. CLANG! BONG! Wobble-wobble-wobble.

Little Pippa came running in her yellow socks. Dust bunnies had gathered under the piano like sleepy grey sheep, and crumbs sat on the rug, waiting for a party. "Grandma comes on Saturday," Pippa said. "Could you clean the living room, please, Wilbur?"

"Clean? Yes. Easy. Mostly," said Wilbur. "Except the living room has Mrs. Figgs in it."

Mrs. Figgs sat in a patch of sunshine, washing one paw with great care. She did not look up. She did not need to. Wilbur's wheels went wobbly.

Wilbur tried anyway. He tiptoed forward, his wheels clicking softly on the floorboards. Mrs. Figgs opened one green eye. Wilbur gave a tiny "Eeep!" and reversed so fast that he tangled himself in a ball of Pippa's red yarn. There he sat, wrapped up like a parcel, with a sad little boop.

That was when Wilbur noticed something. Each time he zoomed, Mrs. Figgs leapt. Each time he crept, she only watched. Just then, a dust bunny rolled slowly out from under the sofa, round and soft as a pillow. Mrs. Figgs's ears swivelled. Her tail began to twitch.

"Slow," Wilbur whispered. "Be slow, like a snail in pyjamas."

He wriggled free of the yarn. He rolled forward, hmm-hmm-hmm, quiet as a whisper. He stopped beside the dust bunny and went schlurp, very gently. The bunny vanished into his belly. Mrs. Figgs blinked, tilted her head, and said, "Mrrrp?"

"Mrrrp," said Wilbur, very softly.

Mrs. Figgs stretched, padded across the rug, and sniffed his blue lid. Wilbur held perfectly still and hummed a low, rumbly hmmmmm. The cat sniffed again. Then, with one big hop, she climbed on top of him, turned around three times, and settled down like a fluffy cushion. Her purr sounded like a kettle warming up on the stove.

"Hmm," said Wilbur. "Now I am a sofa."

So Wilbur cleaned the living room inch by inch, with Mrs. Figgs riding on his back. He nudged crumbs with his brush. He hummed his slow, soft song. Under the piano, the dust bunnies sighed and drifted into his tummy, one by one. Pippa clapped her hands and giggled until she had to sit down on the rug.

On Saturday, Grandma came in, sniffed the clean air, and smiled at the sparkling floor. She had no idea how brave a little robot had been to get it that way.

Now the house is quiet. The lamp glows low and golden. Wilbur's blue light dims to a soft blink, and his brush rests still. Mrs. Figgs curls into a warm, round ball on the rug beside him. Pippa's yarn is tucked away in its basket.

Hush now. The stairs are sleeping. The clock ticks slowly. Goodnight, Wilbur. Goodnight, Mrs. Figgs. Goodnight, sleepy house.

final.title: Wilbur and Mrs. Figgs
final.text:
Wilbur was a robot vacuum cleaner with a round blue body, a whirry little brush, and a very big fear. The fear had whiskers, green eyes, and a fluffy grey tail. Her name was Mrs. Figgs.

Every morning, Wilbur rolled out of his charging dock with a cheerful beep. "Bzzt-bzzt, I am brave, I am brave," he hummed. Then a tail flicked around the corner of the sofa, and Wilbur spun around so fast that he bonked into the umbrella stand. CLANG! BONG! Wobble-wobble-wobble.

Little Pippa came running in her yellow socks. Dust bunnies had gathered under the piano like sleepy grey sheep, and crumbs sat on the rug, waiting for a party. "Grandma comes on Saturday," Pippa said. "Could you clean the living room, please, Wilbur?"

"Clean? Yes. Easy. Mostly," said Wilbur. "Except the living room has Mrs. Figgs in it."

Mrs. Figgs sat in a patch of sunshine, washing one paw with great care. She did not look up. She did not need to. Wilbur's wheels went wobbly.

Wilbur tried anyway. He tiptoed forward, his wheels clicking softly on the floorboards. Mrs. Figgs opened one green eye. Wilbur gave a tiny "Eeep!" and reversed so fast that he tangled himself in a ball of Pippa's red yarn. There he sat, wrapped up like a parcel, with a sad little boop.

That was when Wilbur noticed something. Each time he zoomed, Mrs. Figgs leapt. Each time he crept, she only watched. Just then, a dust bunny rolled slowly out from under the sofa, round and soft as a pillow. Mrs. Figgs's ears swivelled. Her tail began to twitch.

"Slow," Wilbur whispered. "Be slow, like a snail in pyjamas."

He wriggled free of the yarn. He rolled forward, hmm-hmm-hmm, quiet as a whisper. He stopped beside the dust bunny and went schlurp, very gently. The bunny vanished into his belly. Mrs. Figgs blinked, tilted her head, and said, "Mrrrp?"

"Mrrrp," said Wilbur, very softly.

Mrs. Figgs stretched, padded across the rug, and sniffed his blue lid. Wilbur held perfectly still and hummed a low, rumbly hmmmmm. The cat sniffed again. Then, with one big hop, she climbed on top of him, turned around three times, and settled down like a fluffy cushion. Her purr sounded like a kettle warming up on the stove.

"Hmm," said Wilbur. "Now I am a sofa."

So Wilbur cleaned the living room inch by inch, with Mrs. Figgs riding on his back. He nudged crumbs with his brush. He hummed his slow, soft song. Under the piano, the dust bunnies sighed and drifted into his tummy, one by one. Pippa clapped her hands and giggled until she had to sit down on the rug.

On Saturday, Grandma came in, sniffed the clean air, and smiled at the sparkling floor. She had no idea how the floor had got so shiny, and Pippa just smiled and said nothing at all.

Now the house is quiet. The lamp glows low and golden. Wilbur's blue light dims to a soft blink, and his brush rests still. Mrs. Figgs curls into a warm, round ball on the rug beside him. Pippa's yarn is tucked away in its basket.

Hush now. The stairs are sleeping. The clock ticks slowly. Goodnight, Wilbur. Goodnight, Mrs. Figgs. Goodnight, sleepy house.

request: My son is getting a new baby sister next week and he's worried we won't have time for him

first_draft.title: Jonah's Clock with a Golden Star
first_draft.text:
Jonah sat on the bottom stair and listened to his house. The kitchen clock went tick. The kettle gave a small, sleepy sigh. Upstairs, a little pile of tiny socks waited for a baby who was coming next week.

"Will we still have time for me?" Jonah asked.

Dad put down the laundry basket and crouched until their eyes were level. "Yes, Jonah. Time with you is one of my favorite things."

Jonah nodded. But his tummy felt tight, like a sock pulled on too far.

That night, he counted in bed. One story. One goodnight kiss. One sleepy hug. "Not enough," he whispered to his bear, Admiral. Admiral's button eyes looked back and said nothing at all.

The next morning, Jonah tried very hard to be helpful. He carried a wobbly stack of diapers to the nursery. Thump! Half of them slid onto the rug. He poured milk for Mom, and it went over the table in a big sploosh.

"Oops," said Mom, reaching for a cloth. "Don't worry about it, sweetheart." Jonah's cheeks went hot. Helping was not working.

So he tried being quiet. He tiptoed past the baby's room, past the kitchen, past Dad's humming. Nobody noticed him at all.

That afternoon, Jonah sat at the kitchen table with a box of crayons. The clock went tick, tock, tick. "Tick, tock," said Jonah. "Who has time for Jonah?"

He drew a big round clock on a sheet of paper. He drew two hands and a bright yellow star at the very top. Then he drew a little bed, a paper boat, and a dinosaur wearing a hat. Each picture was something he liked to do with someone.

"Mom," he said, holding it up. "This is a Jonah Clock. When the long hand touches the star, it's Jonah time. Ten minutes. Just me and you. Or me and Dad."

Mom knelt beside him and looked at the drawing for a long time. "I love it," she said. "Shall we pick the star's time together?"

They chose after dinner, when the sun was low and orange. Dad said yes too. They stuck the picture on the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon. Jonah felt his tight tummy loosen, one sock at a time.

Now the clock's tick sounded like a friend. Jonah had made a plan, and the plan had room for him.

At bedtime, Dad read two stories. Jonah pointed to the star on the fridge through the doorway. "Tomorrow," he said. "Ten minutes."

The hallway light dimmed to a soft glow. The kettle was quiet. The tiny socks waited in their drawer.

"Tick," said the clock, slow and gentle.

"Tock," whispered Jonah, pulling Admiral close.

Dad switched off the lamp. Mom kissed his forehead, warm as toast.

"Goodnight, Jonah," they said together, very softly.

And the clock kept ticking, just for him.

first_draft.title: Captain Dahlia and the Confetti Cannons
first_draft.text:
The fog over Gull Rock was as thick as porridge when two pirate ships sailed out of it, nose to nose. On the left bobbed the Sea Pickle, flying a flag with a grinning lobster. On the right rocked the Brine Biscuit, flying a flag with a crooked crab. Both crews gripped their cutlasses and squinted through the mist.

“Hand over that treasure map!” roared Captain Dahlia Crookshank, twirling her sword so fast it whistled. “Never!” bellowed Captain Xavier Bonemarrow, whose beard was tangled with seashells that clinked every time he shouted. Each captain held half of a torn map, and both halves showed the same wobbly red X on the same faraway island.

“Cannons!” cried Dahlia. “Fire!” KER-POOF! Out burst a cloud of purple confetti that spun over the water and settled on Xavier’s hat like a party guest who had arrived too early. The Sea Pickle crew cheered. The Brine Biscuit crew cheered even louder, because nobody on their ship had ever been showered with confetti before.

“Our turn!” shouted Xavier, and he pulled a lever. FWOOSH! A hundred soap bubbles wobbled across the waves, shimmering pink and gold. One drifted right onto Dahlia’s nose and popped with a tiny, tickly sound. Her parrot, Mustard, sneezed so hard that he tumbled off the rigging and into a bucket.

Then the captains leapt onto a rope bridge between the ships and began a sword duel. Clang! Swish! Dahlia’s blade bent like a cooked noodle and wrapped itself around Xavier’s boot. He hopped on one leg, wobbled, and toppled backward into a heap of seaweed. Dahlia tripped over him, and they both lay there giggling, dripping with weed.

“Well,” said Dahlia, wiping her eyes, “we make a fine pair of pirates.” Then she spotted something. Her half of the map showed a palm tree on the left, and Xavier’s half showed a waterfall on the right. She slid the two halves together and gasped. The palm and the waterfall lined up perfectly, and the X now sat beside a little arrow pointing into the cove.

The two crews rowed ashore together and hopped across the warm sand. Mustard flapped ahead, squawking, “Treasure! Treasure! Squawk!” They followed a winding path between the palm trees, past a splashing waterfall that tickled their toes. Behind a big rock they found a wooden chest with a lock so rusty it looked grumpy.

Xavier tugged. Dahlia tugged. The lid didn’t budge. Then Xavier plucked a spiral seashell from his beard, and it fit the keyhole exactly. Click! The lid creaked open. Inside lay gold-wrapped chocolate coins and a jar of sticky lemon drops. The two crews sat in a circle on the sand, passing the jar around until every pocket was full and every tongue was sweet.

The sun sank into the sea, turning the water the colour of marmalade. The two ships rocked side by side, their lanterns glowing softly. The last bits of confetti drifted over the sand, and the last bubble floated up and up until it was gone. Mustard tucked his head under one wing. Captain Dahlia yawned, and Captain Xavier yawned right back. The waves hushed against the shore. Goodnight, little cove. Goodnight, pirates. Goodnight.

first_draft.title: Ada and the Garden Egg
first_draft.text:
Ada found the egg in the garden, tucked under the big fern where the morning dew still sparkled. It was speckled green and gold, and it was warm, like a loaf fresh from the oven.

"Hello," Ada whispered. The egg gave a tiny crack. Then another. Then a sound came out, a squeaky, hiccupy sound, like a teakettle that had forgotten how to whistle.

"Mum! Mum, the egg is talking!"

Her mum came out with a wooden spoon still in her hand. She knelt down beside Ada and peered at the egg. "Well, I think it wants a name," she said with a smile.

But before Ada could think of one, the egg wobbled, rolled, and bumped right into a flowerpot. Out tumbled a baby dinosaur, no bigger than a loaf of bread. Her skin was the colour of moss, and she had a long, floppy neck and a tail that curled like a question mark.

"Oh no," Ada gasped. "Where is your nest?"

The baby dinosaur blinked. Then she opened her mouth and made a sound like a rusty gate. Hrrrmp! Ada laughed so hard she almost fell over.

They searched the garden together. They looked under the rhubarb leaves, behind the shed, and inside the wheelbarrow. Ada's mum found a muddy welly and a very surprised snail. Ada found a sock, a tennis ball, and a bird's feather. But no nest.

"She must be hungry," said Ada. "What do baby dinosaurs eat?"

They tried some apple slices. The dinosaur sniffed them and sneezed a tiny puff of green glitter. They tried a crust of toast. She wrinkled her nose. Then Ada had an idea. She ran to the compost heap and came back holding a fat, wriggly worm.

The dinosaur's eyes lit up like lanterns. She gobbled the worm up in one happy slurp. Her tail wagged so fast it made a whoosh in the air.

"Now we need to find where she belongs," Ada said softly. She sat down on the grass and looked up at the sky. The clouds were turning pink and orange. "Maybe she came from far away, like the birds that fly south."

The dinosaur climbed into Ada's lap and yawned a huge, wide yawn. Her little eyelids drooped. Ada stroked the soft ridge along her back, and the dinosaur's eyes slowly closed.

Ada's mum sat down next to them. "Look," she whispered. "She's making a nest out of her own blanket." The dinosaur had tugged a corner of the old picnic rug over the flowerpot and was curling up inside it, round and snug.

Ada grinned. "She picked her own home," she said. "Maybe she was just looking for somewhere cosy."

They tucked the rug in tight around her, and the dinosaur gave one last sleepy hrrrmp. Then the garden went quiet, except for the crickets and the soft tick of the cooling day.

Ada tiptoed back to the house, looking over her shoulder. Her mum turned off the porch light. Above the fern, the first star blinked, and somewhere in the garden a small, contented snore drifted up through the dark.

Goodnight, little dinosaur, Ada whispered. Goodnight.

first_draft.title: June and the Wobbly Red Bike
first_draft.text:
The morning sun slid through the curtains of the little blue house on Maple Lane, and June Okonkwo woke up with a wobble in her tummy. Today was the day. Today she would ride her bike without the stabilisers.

Her bike was red, with a silver bell that went ting when she pressed it. Her dad held the back of the saddle while she pedalled along the garden path. The wheels crunched over the gravel. Ting, ting, went the bell.

"Don't let go," June said, looking over her shoulder.

"I've got you," said Dad, puffing a little. "Keep your eyes forward, June. Look where you want to go, not at your feet."

She pedalled. The bike wobbled left. It wobbled right. Then, all at once, it went quite still and wobbly all at the same time, and June's heart thumped like a drum.

"Dad! You're holding me!"

"I let go a little while ago," Dad said softly. "You're doing it yourself."

June gasped. She was riding. All by herself. The wind tickled her cheeks and her hair streamed out behind her like a flag. Then the front wheel bumped over a bumpy stone, and June wobbled, and wobbled, and wobbled, and stopped with a squeak right in front of the hedgehog's hole.

A small brown face peeped out. Its nose twitched. "Well," said the hedgehog in a voice like a creaky gate, "that was a very noisy wobble."

June giggled so hard she nearly fell off. "I'm learning," she said. "Bikes are tricky. They like to wiggle when you're not looking."

"Hmm," said the hedgehog, rolling its eyes. "Bikes are like hedgehogs. They need to feel steady underneath them."

June thought about that. She sat up tall, held the handlebars loosely, and pushed off again. This time she looked at the big oak tree at the end of the lane. Pedal, pedal, pedal. The bike wobbled once, then steadied itself, as if it had found its balance.

At the oak tree she stopped, put her feet down, and grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. Dad came running up, his trainers slapping the path.

"You did it!" he cheered. "You rode all the way on your own!"

"I wobbled a lot," June admitted. "But I kept going anyway."

"That's the best way," said Dad, ruffling her hair. "Wobbling is just part of learning."

That evening, June sat in the bath with bubbles up to her chin, and she wiggled her toes and sang a wobbly song about bikes and hedgehogs. Dad sat on the edge of the tub and listened.

Then it was time for bed. June climbed under her quilt, and the moon peeped through the window like a friendly silver coin. Downstairs, the kettle hummed softly. Outside, the oak tree whispered in the breeze.

June yawned a big, slow yawn. Her legs still felt like they were pedalling, round and round, gentle and slow.

She closed her eyes. Round and round. Soft and slow. Goodnight, little rider.

first_draft.title: Wenceslas and the Shrinking Puddle
first_draft.text:
Wenceslas was a scruffy brown dog with floppy ears and four very muddy paws. He loved puddles more than biscuits, more than squeaky toys, and almost more than his supper. When the rain stopped, he raced out the back door with his tail whirling like a windmill, ready for a splash.

"Wenceslas! Wipe those paws!" called Mina from the kitchen window. But Wenceslas had already found the biggest puddle in the garden. He leapt in with a SPLOSH, then a SPLOSHY SPLOSH, and water sprayed over the tulips and onto Mina's yellow boots.

"You are the muddiest dog in the whole village," Mina said, laughing, though she was not cross at all. Wenceslas wagged so hard his whole back end wiggled.

That afternoon the sun came out, warm and golden. Wenceslas trotted down the garden path to visit his puddle, but it was smaller. Its edges had crept back, like a blanket slowly being pulled away. In a dip beside the fence sat a tiny green frog, blinking anxiously in the last little pool of water.

"Oh dear," said Wenceslas, though it came out as a small, worried woof. "You're going to get stuck, little frog."

The frog hopped once, then sat down again. The big puddle was on the far side of the compost heap, and between them lay a long stretch of dry, cracked earth. Frogs cannot hop across dry ground for long, and the sun was getting hotter.

Wenceslas tried everything he could think of. He barked, which made the frog jump in fright. He lay down beside the pool, but his tummy was too big and he pushed most of the water away. He pawed at the puddle, and the drops just splashed out of reach.

He sat down. He wagged. He thought. His nose twitched at the smell of damp earth. Then his ears pricked up. Under the dry top layer, the soil was cool, dark and soft.

So Wenceslas began to dig. Scritch, scratch, scritch! Earth flew over his shoulder and mud stuck to his nose. He dug a long, wiggly channel from the little pool toward the big puddle, shallow and careful. Slowly, a thin, bright thread of water began to trickle along it.

The frog watched. Then, with one happy hop, it jumped onto the wet path, and then another, and another, splashing all the way down the channel until it reached the big puddle with a loud plop.

Wenceslas flopped down in the grass, panting and filthy. His paws ached, and a small part of him was sad that the sun had drunk up his favourite pool. But when the frog peeked out from the big puddle and croaked a happy hello, his tail gave one proud thump.

Mina came down the path with a towel and stopped, staring at the muddy trench. "Wenceslas," she said, "what have you been up to?" The dog only sneezed, showering her with mud droplets. "Right," she sighed, "bath time."

That evening, Wenceslas lay by the warm stove with a towel still around him, his fur smelling of soap. Outside, the sky grew soft and grey. Then pit-pat, pit-pat, a gentle rain began to tap on the window.

Wenceslas lifted one ear. Somewhere in the garden, a new puddle was forming, round and shiny, waiting for morning.

He sighed, tucked his nose under his tail, and let the rain sing him to sleep. Goodnight, Wenceslas. Goodnight, little frog.

first_draft.title: Fig and the Moonwick Night Train
first_draft.text:
The Moonwick Night Train left the station with a long, slow sigh. Its wheels went clickety-clack, clickety-clack, like someone counting sheep in a whisper. Outside, the fields rolled past in soft grey waves, and the stars hung low over the hedges, as if they wanted a closer look at the train.

Fig was the train's lamp-keeper. Every hour she walked up and down the carriages, checking that each little lamp still glowed like warm honey. She wore a woolly green hat, carried a ticket punch shaped like a crescent moon, and tried very hard to hide her yawns.

"Lamps are glowing. Tickets are punched. The engine is humming," she whispered to herself. "Nothing urgent tonight. Nothing urgent at all."

In the fourth carriage, an old man sat by the window with his coat buttoned up to his chin. His name was Hector, and his face was as creased as a letter read many times. He was patting the seat beside him, then patting his coat pockets, then patting the seat again.

"Good evening, Hector," said Fig softly. "Are you comfortable?"

"Almost," said Hector. "I've lost my spectacles. Without them the world goes fuzzy around the edges. My granddaughter gave me a book, and I promised her I would finish it before we reach the sea."

Fig sat down opposite him. The seat smelled of peppermints and rain. The train swayed gently from side to side, and the lamps flickered like sleepy fireflies.

They searched together. Fig peeked under the cushions and found a pencil stub, a button shaped like a star, and a crumb that had been there since the summer. Hector checked his coat and found a folded map, a ticket from last Tuesday, and half a biscuit wrapped in paper. He sighed and offered Fig the biscuit. She took it, but the spectacles were still lost.

Fig knelt down and peered beneath the seat, where dust bunnies had gathered in the corners. Nothing there but a sleepy moth, tapping softly against the little lamp. "Perhaps they fell through a gap," Hector murmured. "Perhaps they're gone for good."

Fig didn't want that to be true. She sat back on her heels and closed her eyes. Clickety-clack went the wheels. Hum went the window. Tap, tap went the moth. Fig listened, and while she listened, she remembered something her grandmother used to say: when you can't find a thing, go back to the last place you were looking.

She opened her eyes. "Hector, what were you doing just before you started patting your pockets?"

Hector thought for a long moment. "I was looking at the moon," he said. "It's been following us across the fields all evening. It's rather a grand moon."

"So you were looking up," said Fig slowly. "Up at the sky."

Hector frowned, then lifted his hand and touched his own forehead. His fingers stopped. Something small and round was resting there, right above his eyebrows, glinting in the golden lamplight.

"Well, I'll be," Hector chuckled. "They've been up here all along, keeping watch on the moon."

Fig giggled so hard that the moth flew off in a huff. Hector laughed too, a warm, wheezy laugh, and he slid the spectacles down onto his nose. Slowly, the world came back into focus: the silver fields, the dark silhouettes of trees, and the moon, round and bright, sailing beside the window as if it had been waiting for them.

"Thank you, Fig," Hector said. "You found what I couldn't."

"You found it yourself," Fig said. "I only asked where you'd been looking."

Hector opened his book and read a page out loud, his voice low and steady. Fig leaned back against the cushions. Her yawn was no longer hidden, and she didn't mind one bit.

At the far end of the train, the engine began to slow. The wheels changed their tune: clickety... clack... clickety... clack. The sleeping village came into view, with its roofs silver with moonlight and one window glowing in a cottage where someone was already in bed.

Fig rose and walked slowly down the carriage. She turned each little lamp down, one by one, until the light was no brighter than a candle left burning in another room. Hector closed his book and tucked it under his arm. He sank into the seat with a contented sigh.

"Shall I wake you at the sea?" Fig asked quietly.

"Wake me only if the sea is very beautiful," Hector said, his eyes already drifting closed behind his spectacles.

Fig smiled and pulled her green hat down over her ears. The train rocked gently, clickety-clack, clickety-clack, slower now, softer now, like a song being hummed under a blanket.

Outside, the stars leaned in close. The fields drifted into shadow. The moon kept its quiet watch over the carriages.

Clickety... clack... clickety... clack...

Goodnight, little train. Goodnight, moon. Goodnight, Hector. Goodnight, Fig.
